## Learning goals


1. Identify an appropriate [scientific hypothesis]{.alert} that addresses a biological question
3. Identify an appropriate [Null Hypothesis]{.alert} that tests a scientific hypothesis
4. Identify an [Alternative Hypothesis]{.alert}
4. Understand the practice of [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert} (NHST)
5. Explain the meaning of a [$P$-value]{.alert}
7. Explain the concepts of [false positives]{.alert} and [false negatives]{.alert} and why they happen


## Scientific hypotheses posit testable explanations

Why are leaves green? [*Green pigments evolved to maximize photosynthetic rates.*]{style="color: white;"}

How does the immune system tell self from non-self? [*Immune cells that react to the body's own molecules are eliminated during development.*]{style="color: white;"}

What causes type 2 diabetes? [*A food environment that is calorie-dense but low in accessible healthy options drives chronic caloric excess, leading to insulin resistance.*]{style="color: white;"}

What is causing accelerating extinction of Hawaiian honeycreepers? [*Avian malaria, spread by introduced mosquitoes now reaching high-elevation forests as climate warms.*]{style="color: white;"}

## Scientific hypotheses posit testable explanations

Why are leaves green? *Green pigments evolved to maximize photosynthetic rates.*

How does the immune system tell self from non-self? *Immune cells that react to the body's own molecules are eliminated during development.*

What causes type 2 diabetes? *A food environment that is calorie-dense but low in accessible healthy options drives chronic caloric excess, leading to insulin resistance.*

## We test hypotheses by making predictions

If $X$, then $Y$

::: {.fragment}
*If* green pigments maximize photosynthesis, *then* substituting other pigments will reduce photosynthetic rate.
:::

::: {.fragment}
*If* Incompatible Insect Technique reduces mosquito populations, *then* endangered honeycreeper populations will rebound.
:::


## Scientific versus statistical hypotheses

Scientific and statistical hypotheses are related, but for [statistical hypotheses]{.alert} to be useful, they must be more ***precise***

## Identify a [Null Hypothesis]{.alert}

A [statistical hypothesis]{.alert} has two parts, first:

> A [null hypothesis]{.alert} is a specific statement about a population parameter made for the purposes of argument. A good [null hypothesis]{.alert} is a statement that would be interesting to reject

## A [null hypothesis]{.alert} must be specific

The proportion of a times a fair coin lands on heads is $\mathbf{p = 0.5}$

There is **no difference** in the proportion of red M&Ms in bags sold at Sams versus those sold at Costco

Patients in the treatment group have the **same probability** of contracting a disease as patients in the control group

## A [null hypothesis]{.alert} should be "interesting" to reject


::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}

This is somewhat subjective, but there are lots of trivial null hypotheses that aren't worth studying.

<br>

For example: There are 0 trees in Hawaiʻi<br>
[foo]{style="color: white;"}

<br>

This is specific, but trivially easy and uninteresting to reject
:::

::: {.fragment}

This is somewhat subjective, but there are lots of trivial null hypotheses that aren't worth studying.

<br>

For example: The growth rate of native trees in Hawaiʻi are the same as their con-generic relatives from continents

<br>

This is specific, *and* interesting to reject
:::

:::

## Identify an [Alternative Hypothesis]{.alert}

Part two of the [statistical hypothesis]{.alert} is:

> The [alternative hypothesis]{.alert} includes all other feasible values for the population parameter besides the value stated in the [null hypothesis]{.alert}

## An [alternative hypothesis]{.alert} is not specific

The proportion of a times a fair coin lands on heads is not $p = 0.5$

There is a difference in the proportion of red M&Ms in bags sold at Sams versus those sold at Costco

Patients in the treatment group have a different probability of contracting a disease as patients in the control group

## Identifying [null]{.alert} and [alternative]{.alert} hypothesis

## Identifying [null]{.alert} and [alternative]{.alert} hypothesis

First a note on naming conventions

$H_0$: pronounced "H-naught" or "H-zero" is the convention for the [null hypothesis]{.alert}

$H_\mathrm{A}$:is the convention for the [alternative hypothesis]{.alert}

::: {.fragment}

So...

$H_0$: Mean difference (after - before) in sedimentation rate for the group receiving noni and the placebo group will be **identical**

$H_\mathrm{A}$: Mean difference (after - before) in sedimentation rate for the group receiving noni and the placebo group will be **different**

:::

## Learning goals

1. Identify an appropriate [scientific hypothesis]{.alert} that addresses a biological question $\checkmark$
3. Identify an appropriate [Null Hypothesis]{.alert} that tests a scientific hypothesis $\checkmark$
4. Identify an [Alternative Hypothesis]{.alert} $\checkmark$
4. Understand the practice of [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert} (NHST)
5. Explain the meaning of a [$P$-value]{.alert}
7. Explain the concepts of [false positives]{.alert} and [false negatives]{.alert} and why they happen

## Identify a [Null Hypothesis]{.alert}

> A [null hypothesis]{.alert} is a specific statement about a population parameter made for the purposes of argument. A good [null hypothesis]{.alert} is a statement that would be interesting to reject

## A null hypothesis must be specific and should be "interesting" to reject

**For example:**

There are 0 trees in Hawaiʻi

This is specific, but trivially easy and uninteresting to reject

## A null hypothesis must be specific and should be "interesting" to reject

**For example:**

The growth rate of native trees in Hawaiʻi are the same as their con-generic relatives from continents

This is specific, *and* interesting to reject

## Identify an [Alternative Hypothesis]{.alert}

> The [alternative hypothesis]{.alert} includes all other feasible values for the population parameter besides the value stated in the null hypothesis

## An alternative hypothesis is not specific

**For example**:

The growth rate of native trees in Hawaiʻi are *different* than their con-generic relatives from continents

## Naming conventions

$H_0$: pronounced "H-naught" or "H-zero" is the convention for the [null hypothesis]{.alert}

$H_\mathrm{A}$:is the convention for the [alternative hypothesis]{.alert}

## Identifying [null]{.alert} and [alternative]{.alert} hypothesis

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

What is [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}?

::: {.fragment}

It asks the question:

> What would be the probability of observing the sample estimate, or a more extreme estimate, if the [null hypothesis]{.alert} were true?

::: {.incremental}
- If that probability is small, we say "we reject the null hypothesis"
- If that probability is not small, we say "we fail to reject the null hypothesis"
:::

:::

::: {.fragment}
The sample estimate of interest depends on the scientific and null hypotheses
:::


## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

The sample estimate of interest depends on the scientific and null hypotheses

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "4in"


p <- gnoni
p$layers[[1]]$aes_params$alpha <- 0.5


est <- group_by(dat, group) |>
    summarize(ybar = mean(sed))
ann <- data.frame(x = est$ybar, y = 0.5, group = est$group,
                  lab = c("bar(Y)['yes noni']",
                          "bar(Y)['no noni']"))

ydiff <- p + 
    geom_vline(est, mapping = aes(xintercept = ybar, color = group), 
               size = 1.5) +
    geom_label(data = ann,
               mapping = aes(x = x, y = y, label = lab),
               parse = TRUE, hjust = "left", nudge_x = 0.1,
               size = 5) +
    geom_segment(data = data.frame(group = "placebo"),
                 mapping = aes(x = ann$x[1], xend = ann$x[2],
                               y = 0.6, yend = 0.6),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "npc"), ends = "both"),
                 size = 1.5) +
    geom_label(data = data.frame(group = "placebo"),
               x = -2, y = 0.45, label = expression(bar(Y)["diff"]),
               fill = "white", size = 5) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4.5, 2.75), ylim = c(0, 0.55), clip = "off")

ydiff
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- $H_0$: The mean of *change in sedimentation rate* is the same across the two groups
- $H_A$: The mean is not the same

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
::: {.pause-think}
What is the estimate of interest?
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The estimate of interest:**

$\bar{Y}_\text{diff} = \bar{Y}_\text{yes noni} - \bar{Y}_\text{no noni}$
:::

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

> What would be the probability of observing the sample estimate, or a more extreme estimate, if the [null hypothesis]{.alert} were true?

::: {.fragment}
When doing [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}, the specific sample estimate we use is called a [test statistic]{.alert}
:::

::: {.fragment}
Here we decided the [test statistic]{.alert} is $\bar{Y}_\text{diff}$
:::

::: {.fragment}
How do we get the probability distribution of the [test statistic]{.alert} $\bar{Y}_\text{diff}$?
:::

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

How do we get the probability distribution of the [test statistic]{.alert} $\bar{Y}_\text{diff}$?

> In many *many* ***many*** hypothetical repeated studies, where the [null hypothesis]{.alert} is TRUE, what would be the distribution of [test statistics]{.alert}?


::: {.fragment}
many *many* ***many*** hypothetical repeated studies where the null is TRUE gives us the [sampling distribution]{.alert} of test statistics "under the null"
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align: center;"}
"The Null Distribution"
:::

## Simulating a sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
"The Null Distribution"
:::

## Simulating the null distribution {.top-align}

```{r}
#| label: null-dist
#| cache: true
#| echo: true

# repeatedly shuffle the groups to make a null distribution
all_null <- replicate(1000, {
    noni_null <- noni_dat
    noni_null$group <- sample(noni_null$group)

    ybars_null <- group_by(noni_null, group)
    ybars_null <- summarize(ybars_null, ybar = mean(sed))
    test_stat_null <- diff(ybars_null$ybar)
    test_stat_null
})
```

## Simulating the null distribution {.top-align}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 2
#| out-width: "5in"

null_dist <- data.frame(test_stat_null = all_null)

ggplot(null_dist, aes(x = test_stat_null)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)))
```

## Simulating the null distribution {.top-align}

TO-DO: go back to the bag example and think about putting all data in the bag and scrambling it


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 2
#| out-width: "5in"

# add the observed test statistic
ybars <- group_by(noni_dat, group)
ybars <- summarize(ybars, ybar = mean(sed))
test_stat <- diff(ybars$ybar)
```

## Simulating the null distribution

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 2
#| out-width: "5in"

ggplot(null_dist, aes(x = test_stat_null)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density))) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = test_stat,
               color = "red", size = 1)
```

## Simulating the null distribution

> In many many **many** hypothetical repeated studies, where the [null hypothesis]{.alert} is TRUE, what would be the distribution of [test statistics]{.alert}?

From that [sampling distribution]{.alert} of test statistics, we can calculate the probability of observing the test statistic, or a more extreme value

That probability is:

```{r}
#| echo: true

mean(null_dist$test_stat_null > test_stat |
         null_dist$test_stat_null < -test_stat)
```

This probability has a special name: the [P-value]{.alert}

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

Null Hypothesis Significance Testing asks the question:

> What would be the probability (the [P-value]{.alert}) of observing the test statistic, or a more extreme value, if the [null hypothesis]{.alert} were true?

::: {.incremental}
- If the [P-value]{.alert} is small, we say "we reject the null hypothesis"
- If the [P-value]{.alert} is not small, we say "we fail to reject the null hypothesis"
- How small is small enough?
:::

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
**How small of a [P-value]{.alert} is small enough?**
:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}
Answer: depends on the desired [significance level]{.alert}
:::

::: {.incremental}
- we write the significance level as $\alpha$
- in biology, $\alpha$ is often 0.05
- remember 95% Confidence Intervals? Same thing as $\alpha = 0.05$
:::

## Can we reject the null?

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "4in"

ydiff
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- $H_0$: The mean of *change in sedimentation rate* is the same across the two groups
- Test statistic: $\bar{Y}_\text{diff} = \bar{Y}_\text{yes noni} - \bar{Y}_\text{no noni}$
- Test statistic: $\bar{Y}_\text{diff} =$ `r round(test_stat, 2)`
- P-value: 0

Yes!  At significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, we reject the null that noni has no impact on sedimentation rate
:::
:::

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}: the steps

1. State $H_0$ and $H_A$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. Generate the null distribution
5. Calculate the P-value
6. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if the P-value is less than or equal to $\alpha$ ($p \le \alpha$)
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if P-value is greater than $\alpha$ ($p > \alpha$)

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}: frequent questions

Here is a more typical null distribution and test statistic:

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2.75
#| out-width: "5in"

ybar <- 0
se <- 1

p <- ggplot(data.frame(x = ybar + 3.75 * c(-se, se)), aes(x)) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    xlab(expression("Test stat if"~H[0]~"is true")) +
    ylab("density") +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                  args = list(mean = ybar, sd = se),
                  xlim = ybar + 2.2 * c(-se, se),
                  geom = "area", fill = "blue", alpha = 0.5) +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                  args = list(mean = ybar, sd = se),
                  xlim = ybar + c(-3.75 * se, -2.2 *se),
                  geom = "area", fill = "orange") +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm,
                  args = list(mean = ybar, sd = se),
                  xlim = ybar + c(2.2 * se, 3.75 *se),
                  geom = "area", fill = "orange") +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = ybar, sd = se)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = ybar + 2.2 * se, size = 1) +
    annotate("label", 4, 0.45, label = "Observed test stat = 2.2", 
             hjust = "right") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.47))

p
```

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}: frequent questions

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 2.25
#| out-width: "5in"

p
```

The [P-value]{.alert} is the sum of the probabilities in the two [orange]{style="color: orange;"} regions
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.r-stack}

:::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="2"}

::::: {.fragment fragment-index="0"}
**Question:** If the test statistic = -2.2, why is the P-value the sum of both [orange]{style="color: orange;"} regions?
:::::

::::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
- Because $H_0$ is no difference, and $H_A$ is *any* difference
- This type of alternative hypothesis is called a "two tailed" test
:::::

::::

:::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="4"}

::::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index="2"}
**Question:** Why is the P-value the probability of "the test statistic ***or a more extreme value***"?
:::::

::::: {.fragment fragment-index="3"}
- Because if the null distribution is [continuous]{.alert}, the probability of the exact test statistic will be 0!
- We need an *area under the curve* for a non-zero probability
:::::

::::

:::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="6"}

::::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index="4"}
**Question:** If we reject $H_0$ at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ does that mean our [scientific hypothesis]{.alert} was correct?
:::::

::::: {.fragment fragment-index="5"}
- No, causation is not proven, we just rejected the null at $\alpha = 0.05$
- Also we might have **incorrectly** rejected the null!
:::::

::::


:::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index="6"}

**incorrectly** how?

::::

:::

:::
:::



## Errors in hypothesis testing

There are two types of errors in hypothesis testing

1. Rejecting the null hypothesis when it's true ([false positive]{.alert})

2. Not rejecting the null hypothesis when it's false ([false negative]{.alert})

## [False positive]{.alert}: Rejecting a true null

::: {.incremental}
* This happens with probability $\alpha$
* Pr[False Positive] is independent of sample size
* Called a "[Type I error]{.alert}"
* You can decrease your false positive rate by decreasing $\alpha$
:::

## [False negative]{.alert}: Failing to reject a false null

::: {.incremental}
* Pr[False Negative] depends on sample size, effect size, and precision
* Also called a "[Type II error]{.alert}"
* Increases with decreasing $\alpha$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Statistical power]{.alert} = 1 - Pr[False Negative]

:::: {.incremental}
- You can increase statistical power by increasing your sample size and measurement precision
::::
:::

## Errors

 Null Hypothesis Test Decision  | $H_0$ True  | $H_0$ False
------------------|----------|----------
 Reject $H_0$        | [Type I]{.alert}   | no error
 Do not reject $H_0$ | no error | [Type II]{.alert}

::: {.fragment}
lower $\alpha$ reduces Type I error rate, but raises Type II error rate
:::

::: {.fragment}
both are errors! many methods today choose $\alpha$ to minimize all error, but this is complex.
:::

## Effects of sample size

If $H_0$ is true, sample size has no effect

If $H_0$ is false, statistical power increases with sample size

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "70%"

library(pwr)
power <- pwr.t.test(n = 2:512, d = 0.5, sig.level = 0.05, power = NULL,
                    type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")

df <- tibble(n = rep(2:512, 2), power = c(rep(0.05, 511), power$power),
             group = rep(c("H0 True", "H0 False"), each = 511)) |>
    mutate(
        group = factor(
            group,
            levels = c("H0 True", "H0 False"),
            labels = c(expression(H[0]~True), expression(H[0]~False))
        )
    )

ggplot(df, aes(n, power, color = group)) +
    facet_grid(cols = vars(group), labeller = label_parsed) +
    geom_line(show.legend = FALSE, size = 4) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = c(8, 64, 512)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    xlab("Sample size") +
    ylab(expression(
        paste("Probability of rejecting ", italic(H)[0]))) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 24)
    )
```
